solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Article in class: you look briefly

indicators.note: something that is in a place is enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a caste is a social class
the indefinite article
old form of 'you'

explanation.surface: A teacher tells a pupil to glance quickly at a piece of writing handed out in class.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon marks where the wordplay ends; YE is the old second-person pronoun, a crossword favourite for 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast an eye over something is an idiom for taking a quick glance at it.

clue.text: For whom fancy nicety is too much?

definitions.text: For whom fancy nicety is too much?

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A question about the kind of person who cannot abide elaborate refinement and politeness.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in faN(CY NIC)ety, and the whole clue also describes it: a CYNIC scoffs at fancy niceties.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sceptical of good intentions sneers at elaborate politeness, finding such refinement excessive and insincere.

clue.text: If consulted, told to develop town

indicators.note: to develop something is to change it into a new form, so the letters take a new shape

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asked for advice would say the town ought to be developed.
explanation.walkthrough: All fifteen letters of 'If consulted, told' are rearranged; the comma is just punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: Sutton Coldfield is a real English town on the northern edge of Birmingham in the West Midlands.

clue.text: Search engine and exhaust in an Oxfordshire town

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: taken as written
Microsoft's search engine
to do someone in or do them up is to tire them out; 'do' can mean exhaust

explanation.surface: A town in Oxfordshire apparently notable for web searching and car exhaust fumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exhaust' suggests car fumes, but it is the verb for tiring someone out. Abingdon lies on the Thames just south of Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Abingdon is a market town on the Thames, south of Oxford, historically the county town of Berkshire.

clue.text: Urge to cross island, small one

indicators.note: to cross something can mean to span it from side to side, so one piece stretches across and around another

parts.note: to egg someone on is to urge them
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to make the crossing to a little island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small one' reads as a minor island, but it points to the Small Isles, a named group of Hebridean islands.
explanation.definitionFit: Eigg is one of the Small Isles in Scotland's Inner Hebrides, so it is literally one of the group called small.

clue.text: Artist celebrity cutting veal evenly, with roll

indicators.note: to cut into something is to go inside it, so one piece enters another
evenly points to the even-numbered positions, so only those letters are kept

parts.note: second and fourth letters of the meat
a big name is a celebrity
a roll is a list of names

explanation.surface: A famous chef slices veal into even portions and serves it with a bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artist' is broad here: the answer is a specialist craftsperson. 'roll' is not bread but a roll of names.
explanation.definitionFit: An enamellist is a craftsperson who decorates metal or glass with fused vitreous coatings, a kind of artist.

clue.text: Drink with university publishers and secretary

parts.note: Cambridge University Press
a personal assistant

explanation.surface: An office tea break shared with the university press staff and a secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: CUP is the standard abbreviation for Cambridge University Press.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea, the everyday hot beverage.

clue.text: Spoil function, getting formal

parts.note: cosine, a trigonometric function
set as in fixed and prescribed, like a set speech

explanation.surface: An occasion is ruined when it turns stiff and formal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoil' looks like ruin, but it means pamper; 'function' is maths, not a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil a child is to pamper and indulge them excessively, the same as treating them with fond care.

clue.text: Unwanted acquisition, wrong iPod chosen by girl

indicators.note: letters that are wrong are in the incorrect order and need sorting out

parts.note: taken as written
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl picked the wrong music player and now regrets buying it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chosen' reads as a verb in the surface but is anagram material alongside 'iPod'.
explanation.definitionFit: A poisoned chalice is an idiom for a prize or job that seems desirable but brings trouble to whoever receives it.

clue.text: Correction — approval by millions in depression

parts.note: saying amen expresses agreement

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: a dent is a hollow in a surface
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A fix to a bill is voted through by millions during an economic slump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' suggests an economic slump, but it is a physical hollow in a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An amendment is an alteration made to put right or improve a text, such as a change to a law.

clue.text: Cricket team, we hear, securing amateur's contract?

indicators.note: what we hear is what is spoken, so a word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: knotting is tying, making secure
a ham is an amateur, as in ham radio or ham actor
to hire is to engage under contract

explanation.surface: Gossip that a cricket club is signing an amateur player to a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first sound changes spelling: the silent K of the tying word drops away. Nottinghamshire is an English county with a first-class cricket side.
explanation.definitionFit: Nottinghamshire County Cricket Club plays in England's first-class County Championship, so the county name stands for the side.

clue.text: Bird taps branch, removing tip

indicators.note: taking off the tip means cutting away the end letter, here the front one

parts.note: taps are marked C and H for cold and hot
a bough is a tree branch

explanation.surface: A woodpecker-like bird knocks on a branch after snapping its end off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taps' looks like a verb, but it means the two basin taps, C and H; the first letter of BOUGH goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The chough is a red-billed member of the crow family found on sea cliffs.

clue.text: Come again following setback: perhaps again cross some cattle

indicators.note: after a setback something is sent back, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: 'Come again?' and 'Eh?' both ask someone to repeat
RE- is a prefix meaning again, so 'perhaps' marks it as an example
to ford a river is to cross it

explanation.surface: After a setback, someone tries again to drive cattle across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come again' is a request to repeat, which is EH; turned back it becomes HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereford is a breed of red-and-white beef cattle, named after the English county.

clue.text: With rapid progress on the way, could it improve transparency?

definitions.text: With rapid progress on the way, could it improve transparency?

parts.words: With rapid progress on the way, could it improve transparency?
parts.note: surface reading: whether speeding things along might make an organisation more open
setter's reading: driving fast along a road, with a fluid that clears the glass in front of the driver

explanation.surface: A question whether fast-tracking reforms would make government more open and accountable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transparency' suggests openness in public life, but it means seeing clearly through a windscreen while motoring.
explanation.definitionFit: The fluid sprayed onto a car's windscreen cleans the glass, letting the driver see through it more clearly.

clue.text: Very tiny rodents consuming Carl's old nuts

indicators.note: to consume is to take inside, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: mice are small rodents

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, and crazy letters are scrambled into a new order

parts.note: the name and possessive S, plus O for old

explanation.surface: Minute mice nibble away at nuts belonging to Carl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' is not food but the anagram signal; the letters of CARLS plus O go inside MICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on a microscale is extremely small, measured at a level visible only through magnification.

clue.text: Count having had unexpectedly included host of party

indicators.note: to be included is to be placed within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: to matter is to count, be important

indicators.note: something unexpected turns out differently, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nobleman unexpectedly found himself hosting a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a nobleman but is the verb meaning be important.
explanation.definitionFit: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the famous character presides over the endless tea party.

clue.text: Here you might catch top dog

indicators.note: 'Here' puns on hear, and to catch a word is to hear it spoken

parts.note: a peak is a top or summit

explanation.surface: Advice on where to find the best dog, perhaps at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top dog' reads as a phrase meaning winner, but splits into wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A peke is the short everyday name for a Pekingese, the small long-haired toy breed.

clue.text: Playful and willing? Not all

parts.note: being game for something means being ready and willing
some is less than all

explanation.surface: A question whether everyone is frisky and keen, answered: only a few are.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark splits the halves: the definition and first piece come first, then 'Not all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamesome is an old-fashioned adjective for frolicsome and sportive, full of high spirits and fun.

clue.text: Barrier of course due to party lines

parts.note: a do is a party
L is short for line, doubled for plural

explanation.surface: Of course a barrier went up because of party lines, as in politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' is not a phrase of agreement: it means belonging to a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: In horse racing, a doll is a hurdle or marker placed to close off part of the track, a racecourse-specific sense.

clue.text: Pity uncovered pancreas wound is pussy

indicators.note: wound as the past of wind means twisted round, so the letters are coiled into a new order
stripping off the cover removes the outside, leaving only the inner letters

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lament over a surgical wound to the pancreas that has become infected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wound' is not an injury: it is the past tense of wind, so the letters are twisted round. 'pussy' is an old pet name for a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-haired breed is a domestic feline, and pussy is a familiar affectionate term for any cat.

clue.text: Drink repeatedly over cardiac glitch

indicators.note: to turn something over flips it, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: a spirit
the same drink again

explanation.surface: Heavy drinking over time causes a problem with the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is doubled and the whole is turned over, which in a down clue reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart murmur is an abnormal sound made by blood flow, heard through a stethoscope as a minor irregularity.

clue.text: Loaded p-pipe into brigantines, amidships?

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one piece is put inside another
amidships is the middle of a vessel, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the three central letters of the eleven
a flue is a pipe; the stutter in the clue doubles the first letter

explanation.surface: A stammering sailor describes a pipe being loaded into the middle of sailing ships.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'p-pipe' imitates a stammer, so its synonym is stammered too. 'Loaded' means rich, not cargo-laden.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaded is informal slang for having plenty of money, the same as wealthy or well-off.

clue.text: Tom introducing European goddess

parts.note: a tom is a male cat, a he-cat
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A man named Tom presents a goddess from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a man's name but is a male cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Hecate is the Greek deity of witchcraft, crossroads and the night, a divine figure from mythology.

clue.text: Turn inside out, always on time

parts.note: as in for ever
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Instructions to reverse a garment, always done punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' puts EVER above T.
explanation.definitionFit: Evert is a technical verb, used in anatomy and surgery, for turning an organ outward.

clue.text: One month in paediatry, off and on

indicators.note: switching off then on means skipping one letter and keeping the next

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A doctor spends a month working in children's medicine, but only intermittently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One month' reads as a stint, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Adar is the sixth month of the Jewish civil calendar, falling around February and March.

clue.text: Article covering allusion made about film

indicators.note: to cover is to sit on top of something, so one part comes before the other

parts.note: the definite article

indicators.note: about can mean moved around, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A magazine piece referencing a movie that someone alluded to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' belongs to the anagram material, not the surface grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1991 Ridley Scott road movie starring Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis is a well-known feature picture.

clue.text: Clause clear with executor, extremely so

parts.note: to rid is to clear away

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A will's clause must be made very clear to the executor.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal surface hides the method: only the two ends of 'executor' are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is an extra clause added to a document or bill, a legal term for an appended provision.

clue.text: Hack food?

parts.note: surface reading: the sort of meal a jobbing journalist eats
setter's reading: a hack is also a riding animal, so this is flesh from one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' suggests a hack writer, but it is also a hired or ordinary riding horse; the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The flesh of the equine animal, eaten in some countries, is literally food made from a hack.
